name: Wrought iron (bloomery)
note: ROME HAS THIS at scale. Noricum is famous for it. Soft, tough, weldable, no useful casting.

name: Bronze
note: ROME HAS THIS. Casting, bearings, statuary, instruments.

name: Brass (by cementation)
note: ROME HAS THIS, made by heating copper with calamine and charcoal WITHOUT ever seeing zinc metal. See mat_zinc for why.

name: Lead
note: ROME HAS THIS in enormous quantity from Britannia and Hispania. Cheap. The only common material that survives hot sulfuric acid.

name: Tin
note: ROME HAS THIS from Cornwall and Iberia. Expensive, long haul.

name: Copper (fire refined)
note: ROME HAS THIS. Not pure enough for good conductors; see cap_pure_4N.

name: Silver
note: ROME HAS THIS. Cupellation from galena.

name: Gold
note: ROME HAS THIS. Las Medulas, and Dacia from 106 AD.

name: Mercury
note: ROME HAS THIS from Almaden, an imperial monopoly. Pliny NH 33.118 price-fixes minium at 70 HS per pound.

name: Sulfur
note: ROME HAS THIS from Sicily and the Aeolian islands.

name: Natron (sodium carbonate)
note: ROME HAS THIS from Wadi Natrun. IT IS NOT SALTPETRE. This confusion has wrecked more bootstrap plans than any other single error.

name: Quicklime and slaked lime
note: ROME HAS THIS. Mortar, glass flux, causticising, agriculture.

name: Gypsum plaster
note: ROME HAS THIS.

name: Alum
note: ROME HAS THIS from Melos. Mordant, styptic, sizing.

name: Vitriols (iron and copper sulfates)
note: ROME HAS THIS lying in heaps at pyrite mines as a weathering product, and has no idea what it is for. Feedstock for sulfuric acid.

name: Pyrolusite (manganese dioxide)
note: ROME HAS THIS and already uses it as glassmaker's soap without knowing why.

name: Galena (lead sulfide)
note: ROME HAS THIS everywhere it mines lead. It is also a working semiconductor, which nobody will suspect for 1800 years.

name: Calamine (zinc carbonate/silicate ore)
note: ROME HAS THIS and already smelts it into brass.

name: Asbestos
note: ROME HAS THIS from Cyprus. Pliny describes it. Useful, and it will kill your workers slowly.

name: Emery (Naxos)
note: ROME HAS THIS. Your abrasive for every ground surface in this document.

name: Pozzolana and hydraulic concrete
note: ROME HAS THIS and it is better in seawater than Portland cement. Do not try to improve it.

name: Papyrus
note: ROME HAS THIS. An Egyptian near-monopoly, which is a strategic reason to make paper.

name: Parchment
note: ROME HAS THIS. Durable and dear.

name: Linen
note: ROME HAS THIS. Sailcloth, and the feedstock for rag paper.

name: Wool
note: ROME HAS THIS.

name: Leather
note: ROME HAS THIS. Bellows, seals, gaskets, drive belts.

name: Beeswax
note: ROME HAS THIS. Lost wax casting, luting, acid-proof coating.

name: Tallow
note: ROME HAS THIS. Lubricant for wire drawing and machining.

name: Olive oil
note: ROME HAS THIS in industrial quantity. Soap, lighting, quenching, varnish base.

name: Bitumen and naphtha seeps
note: ROME HAS THIS from Mesopotamia and the Dead Sea. Cable insulation, waterproofing, and the seed of petroleum chemistry.

name: Salt
note: ROME HAS THIS, taxed and strategically controlled. Feedstock for hydrochloric acid and the whole chlor-alkali branch.

name: Soda-lime glass
note: ROME HAS THIS and is genuinely good at it, including deliberately decolourised near-colourless glass.

name: Charcoal
note: ROME HAS THIS. The real ceiling on iron output is forest, not ore.

name: Silk (traded)
note: REACHABLE BUT RUINOUS. Silk Road via Palmyra. Pliny complains of the bullion drain east. Your best early wire insulation.

name: Shellac (traded)
note: REACHABLE BUT DEAR. Indian Ocean trade via Berenice to Muziris, 1 to 3 year lead time. Your best varnish and the only good coil insulation you will have for a century.

name: Natural rubber (Hevea)
note: UNOBTAINABLE. Amazon basin. There is no route to the Americas and there will not be one in your lifetime or your grandchildren's. Every plan that assumes rubber is wrong. Substitutes: gutta percha (also unobtainable), shellac, oiled linen, silk, bitumen, and much later synthetic rubber from coal tar or petroleum, which is a full chemical industry away.

name: Gutta percha
note: UNOBTAINABLE in quantity. Malayan Palaquium latex, not traded west until the 19th century. This is the material that made submarine cables possible historically; you will have to solve undersea insulation another way.

name: Quinine (cinchona)
note: UNOBTAINABLE. Andean. Malaria is endemic around Rome and you cannot treat it. Drain the marshes instead.

name: Chile saltpetre
note: UNOBTAINABLE. Atacama. Your nitrogen comes from nitre beds and, very late, from the electric arc.

name: Potato, maize, tomato, cassava, chilli, cocoa, tobacco, vanilla
note: UNOBTAINABLE. All American. The crops that transformed Old World agriculture are not available to you. Do not plan a population increase around them.

name: Cryolite
note: EFFECTIVELY UNOBTAINABLE. Greenland. Aluminium smelting must use a synthetic fluoride bath made from your own hydrofluoric acid.

name: Platinum in quantity
note: EFFECTIVELY UNOBTAINABLE. The workable placers are Colombian and Uralian. Small quantities may reach you; do not design a process around it.

name: Cast iron
note: Brittle, cheap, castable, 3-4% carbon. Rome has none in the West; Han China has had it for 500 years. Pipes, pots, cannon, machine frames, stoves.

name: Blister steel
note: Bar iron packed in charcoal at about 1000 C for days. Carbon penetrates on the order of a millimetre a day, so use thin bars.

name: Crucible steel
note: Homogeneous, slag-free, and the gate on every cutting tool and every lead screw.

name: Bulk steel (converter and open hearth)
note: Thousands of tonnes instead of kilogrammes. NOTE THE PHOSPHORUS PROBLEM: an acid lining cannot remove it and most European ores carry it, so you need a basic dolomite lining (Thomas and Gilchrist). Knowing this in advance saves you the years it cost Bessemer.

name: High speed and alloy tool steel
note: Tungsten and chromium carbides that hold an edge red hot. Multiplies every machine tool's output several fold.

name: Stainless steel
note: Chromium above about 11% forms a self-healing passive oxide. Chemical plant, cutlery, vacuum systems.

name: Zinc metal
note: CRITICAL PATH AND ALMOST NOBODY SEES IT. Zinc boils at 907 C, below the temperature at which its ore is reduced, so the metal leaves as vapour and reburns at the furnace mouth. That is exactly why Rome makes brass by cementation and has never seen the metal. Seal the retort and condense downward. No zinc, no voltaic pile, no electricity.

name: Nickel
note: Not isolated in antiquity. Coinage, plating, alloy steels, glass-to-metal seals, catalysts.

name: Chromium
note: Aluminothermic or carbon reduction of chromite. Stainless, plating, refractories.

name: Manganese and ferromanganese
note: Deoxidises and desulfurises steel. Rome already mines the ore as a glass decolouriser without knowing it is a metal.

name: Tungsten
note: Melts at 3422 C, the highest of any metal. Lamp filaments, high speed steel, carbide tooling. Needs the arc furnace or hydrogen reduction of the oxide followed by powder sintering.

name: Aluminium
note: Hall-Heroult in a molten fluoride bath. Cryolite is Greenlandic and unobtainable, so you must synthesise the bath from your own hydrofluoric acid. Before electricity aluminium is a precious metal; after it, it is roofing.

name: Magnesium
note: Electrolysis of fused chloride. Light alloys, flashlight powder, reducing agent.

name: High purity graphite
note: Acheson process: heat carbon to about 2500 C. Crucibles and boats that do not contaminate what is melted in them, which is exactly what zone refining needs.

name: Carbon black and lampblack
note: ROME HAS THIS. Ink pigment, and much later the reinforcing filler that makes rubber into tyres.

name: Lead crystal (flint glass)
note: High dispersion. Pair it with crown glass and you get the achromatic doublet, which is what makes a compound microscope beat a single bead.

name: Borosilicate glass
note: Low thermal expansion. The difference between a laboratory and a pile of broken retorts. Needs boron; the Larderello fumaroles in Tuscany are inside the Empire, which is a genuinely lucky break if it holds.

name: Fused quartz
note: Pure silica worked at 1700 to 2000 C with an oxy-hydrogen flame. Indispensable later: you cannot zone refine germanium in anything that contaminates it.

name: Porcelain and high-fired stoneware
note: Kaolin plus feldspar at about 1300 C. Chemical ware, electrical insulators, and an extremely profitable luxury export that Europe chased for six centuries.

name: Portland cement
note: Calcined limestone and clay, ground fine. HONEST NOTE: it is not obviously better than Roman pozzolanic concrete for marine work. Its advantage is consistency and independence from Puteoli.

name: Reinforced concrete
note: Roman concrete is superb in compression and useless in tension. Steel rod fixes that, and the thermal expansion of steel and concrete happen to match closely enough to work, which is luck rather than design.

name: Rag paper
note: Linen rags, retted, limed, beaten by a water-driven stamper, lifted on a wire mould. Cheaper than papyrus, far cheaper than parchment, and the substrate of everything in the information branch.

name: Celluloid (nitrocellulose plastic)
note: The first thermoplastic. Film base, combs, billiard balls. VIOLENTLY FLAMMABLE and it is what made early cinema so dangerous.

name: Camphor (traded)
note: Reachable via the Indian Ocean and Chinese trade, expensive. Needed for celluloid and for smokeless powder.

name: Bakelite (phenol formaldehyde)
note: The first fully synthetic plastic, from coal tar phenol. Electrical insulation, housings, and the thing that makes mass-produced electrical goods possible.

name: Formaldehyde
note: Catalytic oxidation of methanol from wood distillation. Resins, and the first practical tissue preservative.

name: Synthetic rubber
note: YOUR ONLY ROUTE TO RUBBER. Butadiene from petroleum or from alcohol, polymerised. It sits behind a full petrochemical industry, which is why every plan that casually assumes rubber is wrong by about a century.

name: Refined petroleum fractions
note: Mesopotamian and Caucasian seeps are workable without drilling. Fractionate into naphtha, kerosene, gas oil, lubricants, wax and residue. Kerosene lighting alone pays for the plant.

name: Ammonia
note: Ammonia liquor is a by-product of coking coal, so it is nearly free once you coke. Fertiliser, refrigeration, nitric acid via Ostwald oxidation.

name: Chlorine and bleach
note: Bleaching powder ends the field-bleaching bottleneck that limited every textile industry, and hypochlorite makes water safe. Also war gas: be careful whom you teach.

name: Synthetic dyes (aniline)
note: Coal tar to benzene to aniline to mauveine and the rest. Historically this single industry funded organic chemistry, created the first industrial research laboratories, and led directly to pharmaceuticals. Enormously profitable and politically harmless.

name: Nitrocellulose
note: Guncotton and the base of smokeless powder, celluloid and film. Unstable if badly washed; several early factories destroyed themselves.

name: Nitroglycerin and dynamite
note: Absorbed into kieselguhr it becomes handleable. Mining and tunnelling output rises sharply. Also the most likely single thing in this document to kill you and everyone in the building.

name: Glycerol
note: A by-product of soap making that Rome throws away.

name: Artificial ice and mechanical refrigeration
note: Vapour compression with ammonia. Food preservation, meat shipping, brewing year round, and the seed of gas liquefaction and low temperature physics.
